sourceObservations.observations: Lecture 26 title, Fundamentals of Machine Learning I; footer 1, attribution only.
Learning objectives include supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement distinctions and generalization/overfitting/underfitting. These are roadmap promises, not definitions or proofs on this slide.
Contents outline motivations, rule systems, machine-learning taxonomy, supervised nearest neighbors and linear regression. No new technical premise.

Data and experience can address appearance/environment variation that is difficult to enumerate as explicit rules. The motivation does not establish success under arbitrary distribution shift or unlimited data irrelevance; representative examples matter.
Rule systems encode human knowledge in explicit if-then-else conditions; manually curated blacklist illustrates dependence on experts and executable representation.

Actual code lowercases the message, scans free money/click here/win prize/urgent in that list order and returns a string at the first substring match. No token boundaries or semantic synonym matching. The display format left-aligns in minimum width 20 and slices message characters before index 55; the slide output is explanatory rather than proof of exact character truncation.

Lists domain specificity, expert dependency and cognitive/computational mismatch. The universal claim that any domain change requires rewriting the entire rule set is overstrong; a qualified update can retain useful rules. Human recognition knowledge need not be expressible as reliable pixel rules.

Eight by eight grayscale grid with first row [0,0,180,220,220,180,0,0]. Legend explicitly maps 0 to black and 255 to white. Independent unconstrained 8-bit pixels give 256^64 arrays; row-major flattening has 64 entries. The stated bit depth is not universal for every image format.

Code imports Iris, 1-neighbor classifier and train_test_split with random_state=0; no explicit test_size or stratify. It fits training data and prints score formatted .0%, with shown output 97%. Formatting alone cannot infer a unique correct/test count; the repaired question supplies 37/38.

Manual if sepal_length<5 returns setosa immediately; elif petal_length<2.5 also setosa; else versicolor and no virginica branch. The ML code instead uses n_neighbors=5 with the same random_state. The prose says upload data, but the actual local .fit call passes arrays, not a network upload.

Contrasts labeled-example prediction with input-only structure and emphasizes usable representations. Example applications do not make every SLAM or anomaly-detection implementation necessarily an ML unsupervised method.

Taxonomy is introduced by task and kind of feedback, listing supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Architecture family, feature storage type and prediction timing do not define these three categories.

Supervised learning uses input/target pairs. Force and slip features give grasp success class 0 in blue and failure class 1 in red; the new star lies inside blue, so predicts class 0. Prediction is not guaranteed success on every future unseen case.

Classification outputs discrete labels including binary and multiclass; regression outputs continuous numerical quantities. Lists kNN/trees/SVM/logistic regression versus linear regression/ridge/SVR and classification versus regression metrics. Numeric coding of a category does not make it regression.

Workflow stores labeled training points, takes a query, finds the closest training point by Euclidean distance and returns its label. Figure has d1 smaller to red class 1 than d2 to blue class 0. The explicit similarity premise says nearby instances in the chosen feature space should have similar outputs.

Voting among k neighbors chooses the most frequent label. Three-neighbor example has two class 1 votes for test 1 and three class 0 votes for test 2. Boundary panels differ for k=1,3,9; no claim of universally increasing unseen accuracy is established.

Terrain inputs are speed in m/s and vibration frequency in Hz; categories are smooth floor 0, gravel 1, grass 2. Low/medium/high vibration rows map to 0/2/1 respectively, not numeric class ordering by vibration.

Actual X rows are [1,10],[1.2,12],[.8,60],[.5,65],[.9,30],[1,35], labels [0,0,1,1,2,2]. X has shape (6,2), y (6,). NumPy arrays, Matplotlib plotting, ListedColormap palette, and sklearn classifier are distinct imports.

One-neighbor model fits the six examples and predicts the batch [[.7,62]], then [0] extracts its first output. Class name dictionary maps 1 to Gravel (Red). No scaling pipeline or known test target appears; a single returned prediction is not measured accuracy.

Printed output is category 1, Gravel (Red), while the actual upper region is purple and low smooth-floor region is reddish. Numeric labels and named regions determine meaning, not the inconsistent color adjectives. Frequency differences dominate the raw-coordinate example, and the nearly horizontal regions do not prove exact horizontal boundaries everywhere.

Linear model yhat=w[0]x[0]+...+w[p]x[p]+b is shown beside a statement of P features: 0 through p inclusive has p+1 entries, so the indexing and stated count require qualification. x is the feature vector; w and b are fitted parameters. The single-feature form is wx+b. Calling all linear regression OLS is overbroad because OLS is one fitting criterion.

The flow diagram initializes wx+b, evaluates mean squared error, adjusts parameters and reaches an optimized fit; the red line approximates rather than interpolates every scatter point. The text calls MSE a sum of squared differences, omitting division by sample count; distinguish SSE from MSE. An iterative illustration does not preclude a direct least-squares solver.

Application table: image pixels to object class; point cloud plus gripper pose to grasp success/failure; torque and velocity time series to actuator fault type; depth image to 3D joint coordinates (regression); LiDAR features to terrain class. The representation and prediction target, not merely numeric inputs, distinguish classification and regression.

Summary repeats learning from data instead of exhaustive manual rules, and supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement learning. Samples as rows and features as columns describes a tabular representation; the statement must not be generalized to every raw image, sequence or graph representation.
Thank-you slide only; printed footer 25. No examinable technical content.

independentAnswers.reasoning: Representative examples may encode useful regularities without enumerating appearances. Distribution relevance is necessary; extra data or parameters alone cannot guarantee transfer.
The expert knows what a defect is but cannot express reliable pixel conditions. This is knowledge-to-rule translation difficulty, not absence of expertise, labels or a rule interpreter.
Manually fixed rules do not update themselves. Review the new pattern, retain useful rules and modify relevant rules while considering false positives; wholesale rewrite is not inevitable.
The code lowercases the text and tests substring membership. urgent occurs inside insurgent, so the urgent branch returns its formatted SPAM string, not a Boolean or the entire input.
Lowercasing gives free product but none of free money, click here, win prize or urgent. String membership neither tokenizes a blacklist phrase nor recognizes no cost as a synonym.
The format <20 is left alignment with minimum field width 20, not truncation. The slice ending at 55 is exclusive, so it includes at most indices 0 through 54.
The displayed 8-bit convention assigns 0 to black and 255 to white. These are pixel intensities, not digit labels or dimensions.
There are 8*8=64 independent locations, each with 256 choices. Multiplication of choices gives 256**64=(2**8)**64=2**512.
The visible grid has 64 entries. Row-major flattening starts with the first row whose first four cells are 0,0,180,220.

37/38=0.9736842105. Percentage formatting multiplies by 100 and rounds to zero displayed decimal places, giving 97%. The count is explicitly supplied, not inferred uniquely from the source rounded output.
The first strict comparison 4.9<5.0 succeeds and returns setosa immediately. The long petal does not reach or override the elif branch.
5.0<5.0 and 2.5<2.5 are both false. The final else returns versicolor; the rule never returns virginica.
Source page 782 explicitly sets n_neighbors=1; the page 783 comparison code sets n_neighbors=5. Random splitting seed and class count do not determine k.
The displayed fit call passes feature and target arrays to a local estimator. No network transfer is shown; the slide word upload must not turn a fitting call into an invented cloud operation.

The introductory distinction concerns labeled targets, unlabeled structure and interaction rewards. Architecture, input numeric type and online versus batch prediction do not by themselves distinguish these feedback paradigms.
The star is inside the blue class-0 region, and class 0 is labeled success. This is a categorical prediction rather than a zero force or a guarantee of physical success.
Terrain type is a discrete category, even if encoded by integers. Grip force in newtons is a continuous quantitative target and therefore a regression formulation.
Exactly one of three named categories is multiclass classification with three classes. A single decision does not make the target binary, and labels are not continuous merely because there are three.

The 1NN flow stores labeled examples and, for a query, finds the nearest individual training point under the selected metric and copies its label. Global frequency and nearest centroid are different rules.
With k=1 and d1<d2, the closest red triangle supplies class 1. Distant blue counts, label averages and a boundary-location requirement do not alter this nearest-point rule.
Euclidean distance is sqrt((3-0)**2+(4-0)**2)=sqrt(25)=5. The alternatives are Manhattan distance 7, squared distance 25, or the difference between coordinate magnitudes 1.
Among [1,0,1], class 1 receives two equal-weight votes and class 0 receives one. The output is class label 1, not vote count 2 or continuous mean 2/3.
The visible k=1,3,9 panels have different boundaries. Changing k changes the local vote, but the figure is not a proof of universally increasing unseen accuracy or a changed class count.
k counts training neighbors consulted for a prediction. Three classes, two features and six stored samples describe other quantities; k need not equal the number of classes.
The source target mapping is 0 smooth floor, 1 gravel, 2 grass. Numeric mapping is authoritative despite a later plot palette inconsistency.
The two measured predictors are robot speed and vibration frequency; the target array encodes terrain category. It is not an image-only task or regression of a class-ID magnitude.
Six rows and two columns give X shape (6,2). One scalar label per row gives y shape (6,), not (2,) or a square matrix.
The fifth feature row is [0.9,30]; the fifth target is 2, which the supplied mapping calls grass. The frequency 30 is an input, not a target or a number of classes.

Squared raw-coordinate distances to [.8,60],[.5,65],[1,35],[.9,30],[1,10],[1.2,12] are 4.01,9.04,729.09,1024.04,2704.09,2500.25. The minimum is 4.01, distance 2.002498 to [.8,60]. Raw mixed-unit feature distance is a numerical metric choice, not a unit-invariant physical distance.
The nearest row has class label 1. Indexing terrain_names with key 1 returns exactly Gravel (Red), not the numeric query frequency or another class name.

The outer brackets form a batch containing one two-feature sample, shape (1,2). Predict returns one label per sample, and [0] selects the first label; neither brackets nor indexing train or change labels.

A predicted label for an unlabeled query demonstrates a model output only. Accuracy needs known reference targets and appropriate evaluation; the query does not convert the training set into held-out data.

Raw Euclidean distance squares numeric coordinate differences. Frequency differences spanning tens can dominate speed differences below one. Arrays do not automatically standardize features or guarantee perfectly horizontal boundaries.
The numeric label dictionary and explicit terrain region names identify the class. Purple/red palette choices do not justify relabeling predictions or reinterpreting a frequency axis as class ID.
NumPy constructs numeric arrays; matplotlib.pyplot performs plotting; KNeighborsClassifier is the estimator. ListedColormap specifies colors rather than performing nearest-neighbor prediction.
w0,w1 and b are fitted model parameters. x0,x1 belong to a particular input and y_hat is the resulting output, not an independent fitted coefficient.
The dot product is 2*3+(-1)*4=2, then adding b=0.5 yields 2.5. Reversing b gives 1.5; dropping the negative sign gives 10.5.
Inclusive contiguous indices 0,...,p contain p+1 entries. For exactly p features the zero-based indices are 0,...,p-1; a separate intercept is not automatically the last measured feature.

A linear prediction function can be fitted by OLS or another criterion such as ridge, also listed on page 787. OLS is unregularized squared-error fitting, not a synonym for every linear-regression method.
Residuals y-yhat are [-1,1,1]. Their squares are [1,1,1], hence SSE=3 and MSE=3/3=1. Unsquared signed residual sums are not squared errors.

For a fixed positive sample count, division by n is multiplication by a positive parameter-independent constant, preserving objective order and minimizers. Objective values need not match; negative scaling reverses order.

The red line is a linear fit that reduces aggregate squared residuals. Non-collinear points cannot all be interpolated by one line, and neither joining points nor assigning color-based classes is the depicted regression objective.

The source depicts one iterative fitting approach, not an exclusivity theorem. A direct least-squares method solves the same squared-error objective via linear algebra; it need not start from the loop initial slope.
The application table pairs point cloud plus gripper pose with binary grasp success/failure. The other three rows are valid separate human-pose, fault and terrain applications, not the grasp row.
Depth-image-to-3D-joint-coordinate prediction has continuous coordinate outputs and is marked regression. The other rows output object, fault or terrain categories.

The table pairs image pixels with object class, and torque/velocity time series with actuator fault type. Swapping task targets or assigning terrain to grasp inputs does not reproduce the displayed rows.

Samples as rows and features as columns is the tabular representation used by this estimator. It does not require raw structured images, sequences or graphs to be that same two-dimensional table or to leak target labels into features.

Nearest-label prediction is useful when chosen feature-distance neighborhoods tend to preserve the relevant output and examples represent the intended task. Equal class counts, matching feature/class counts and row sorting do not establish local semantic similarity.
